title: The old master
hookLine: tradition says Lao Tzu, an archivist, wrote this book at a border gate as he left for the west; historians aren't sure he existed
tomorrow: the Tao that can be told

lines: A GUARD AT A BORDER GATE.
cards: A border post on a mountain road. The guard sees an old man coming and knows him: a keeper of the royal archives, known for his learning, leaving the kingdom for good. The guard doesn't wave him through.
You're going away from the world, he says. Before you go, write down what you know. So the old man stops at the gate and writes.

Then he walks on, and, the story says, nobody knows where he ended his days. That's the story tradition tells about the book this year opens with, the Tao Te Ching, and the man it's credited to: Lao Tzu, the old master.

teach.b: First, a story, not a record.
The tale of the gate comes from an ancient Chinese history by Sima Qian, which is honest about its own doubt: it mentions other men who might have been Lao Tzu and doesn't settle the question.

Historians today aren't sure he existed at all, and some readers think the book gathered sayings from more than one hand. Taoists revere it either way. So here, Lao Tzu means the voice of the book, whoever wrote it down.
Tao means a way, or a road: the path under your feet. In this book it becomes the name for the way everything moves: rivers, seasons, people, the whole world.
The book says again and again that this way can't be fully put into words, then spends its short chapters trying anyway.
Third, written at a gate: at a threshold, by someone halfway out the door, not in a library or a palace. Nothing is kept at a gate; things only pass through.
It suits a book that praises what others overlook: the empty, the low, the quiet.
Fourth, one chapter at a time. Some are only a few lines; on day nine hundred seventy-six, you met one: great things begin small.
This year reads them one a day, quoting the old James Legge translation where it helps and putting the rest in plain words. No hurry.
The old master, in the story, wasn't in one.

how: Taoists revere the Tao Te Ching as a sacred classic, and some readers of other backgrounds keep a copy near and read it a short chapter at a time.

games.q: you're the guard at the gate. a learned keeper of the royal archives is walking out, for good. what do you do?
o: wave him through: it's not your business.
ask him to write down what he knows before he goes.
close the gate so he has to stay.
games.why: in the story the guard asks him to write, and he does: the book is written at the gate, and then he walks on.

practice: Find a doorway, even the open frame between two rooms, and notice that it's mostly nothing: an opening whose whole job is to let things pass.
Breathe slowly and let your thoughts do the same, each one coming up to the threshold and going on through. If you pray, you can pray here, at the edge; if not, just keep watching the opening.

wordCard.voice: Tao. A way, a road, and the name an old Chinese book gives to the way everything moves, a way it says words can't fully hold. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, dào: a way, a road. It's the first character of the Tao Te Ching's first chapter.
